newsitem.title: GERMANY: No Buba money policy change seen through 98-OECD.
newsitem.headline: No Buba money policy change seen through 98-OECD.

text.p: The German Bundesbank is unlikely to change its policy stance up until the end of 1998, when it will hand monetary policy to the European Central Bank, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said.

"Our forecasts are for the period through 1998. During this time-frame we see no reason to change the stance on monetary policy," Grant Kirkpatrick, head of the OECD's Germany group told a news conference on Tuesday.
A second OECD official, Robert Price, director of OECD countries division, said: "At this time we see no reason for a change in monetary policy."
He added however, "That does not mean that the Bundesbank might not see the necessity to change its policy."
Risks to the current monetary policy would be accelerated economic growth and higher wage developments as unemployment stabilises, he said.
Consumer confidence would pick up as a result of various factors, he said, noting high asset values, stablisation on the labour market and continued economic growth.

Turning to foreign exchange issues, Kirkpatrick declined to comment on a fair level for the mark against the dollar. "We have no comment on current dollar rates, but we will still stand by our judgment in the report," he said.
In its report, the OECD noted the mark had depreciated considerably against the dollar compared with the all-time highs seen in 1995, and said this had had a clearly positive impact on exports.
It assumed the mark would retain a lower level.

"The marked effective depreciation of the currency up to Jume 1997 -- which is assumed to continue to obtain over the projection period -- should allow Germany's exports to at least match market growth, in contrast to recent losses," it said.
In the report, completed on July 8 and released today, the Paris-based forecasting unit had also presented a similar view on monetary policy, indicating no rate change was likely.

"With forward rates in the money market showing little sign of any expected tightening of policy and inflation well under control, there is clearly neither the expectation nor justification for a tightening of stance," the report said.
Indeed, the central bank could still have scope to lower policy again if economic growth does not pick up in line with forecasts, the report continued.
"Such a response would be built into a strategy based on matching monetary expansion with potential output," it added.
But the think-tank warned that strong shifts in the value of the mark could influence the central bank's policy stance.
"Although the Bundesbank does not follow an exchange rate target, any substantial shift in the value of the deutschemark would also affect the assessment of monetary conditions."
